name: Stoneham
headline: A shoe town's square, a zoo by the pond,
and a third of the map left to the Fells.
answer: Stoneham is a Middlesex County town of 23,244 people (2020 Census), less than 10 miles northwest of Boston. About a third of its land lies in the Middlesex Fells Reservation. Slightly more than half its homes are single-family. I-93 runs through town, and Boston-bound rail stations sit in Melrose, Winchester and Malden next door.
overview: Early explorers called this land Charlestown End, and Governor Winthrop's party is said to have lunched by Spot Pond in 1632. Farmers settled slowly, and the town broke from Charlestown on December 17, 1725. A stagecoach line on the Medford to Andover Turnpike in 1833 brought house lots, and shoemaking grew from home workshops into more than forty manufacturers. That era left Central Square, with its Second Empire commercial blocks, the 1904 library, and churches lining the north side at Common Street.

A few blocks west of the square, Nobility Hill keeps Italianate, Stick and Queen Anne houses from about 1860 to 1920. The Middlesex Fells covers roughly a third of the town, with Spot Pond, Bear Hill and the Stone Zoo, founded in 1905. Stoneham's housing plan counts slightly more than half its homes as single-family, with much of the rest in larger buildings. The Tri-Community Greenway runs from Gould Street toward Woburn and Winchester.

Much of the Fells land in Stoneham was shaped by the Boston area's water supply. Spot Pond was enlarged into a storage reservoir for communities north of Boston, its level raised by 16 feet, and the Metropolitan District Commission replaced several town pumping stations with a single pumping station and gatehouse, listed on the National Register in 1984. Bear Hill Reservoir, just west of I-93 near the summit of Bear Hill, was built in 1902 and 1903 with two concrete dams and a gatehouse. Spot Pond is no longer part of the drinking water supply, and the John Bottume House, a 19th-century stone house on its eastern shore, now serves as the reservation's visitor center.

housing.text: Stoneham's Housing Production Plan reports that 57.1% of housing units are single-family homes, and nearly half of the remaining multifamily units are in buildings of 20 or more units. About 65% of homes are owner-occupied. The plan points to the town center around Main Street as the area best suited for new housing.

villages.name: Central Square
villages.line: The business district bounded roughly by Main, Central, Church, Winter and Common Streets, with 19th- and early-20th-century commercial blocks.

villages.name: Nobility Hill
villages.line: A residential historic district a few blocks west of Main Street, with houses built between about 1860 and 1920.

villages.name: Farm Hill
villages.line: A hill outside the Fells settled by farmers in the mid-1600s.

villages.name: Haywardville
villages.line: A former mill village along Spot Pond Brook in the Virginia Woods section of the Fells, named for the mid-19th-century Hayward Rubber Works; a trail and a footbridge over an 18th-century dam pass its remains.

commute.text: Stoneham has no rail station of its own; commuter rail stations in Melrose, Winchester, Wakefield and Woburn serve Boston's North Station, and Oak Grove on the Orange Line is about 3.8 miles from Stoneham Center. I-93 runs through town, I-95/Route 128 passes just to the north, and MBTA bus 132 runs between Redstone Shopping Center and Malden Center Station.

places.name: Stone Zoo
places.line: A zoo of about 26 acres near Spot Pond, founded in 1905 and run by Zoo New England.

places.name: Middlesex Fells Reservation
places.line: A DCR reservation with more than 100 miles of trails, a visitor center and an off-leash area at Sheepfold Meadow.

places.name: Spot Pond
places.line: The pond inside the Fells where canoes and kayaks can be rented.

places.name: Tri-Community Greenway
places.line: A paved rail-trail along the Aberjona River from Gould Street in Stoneham to Wedgemere Station in Winchester.

places.name: Central Square
places.line: The historic downtown, with Second Empire blocks, the 1904 Stoneham Public Library and the 1939 town hall.

places.name: Boston and Maine Railroad Depot
places.line: An 1895 single-story brick depot on a granite foundation, with large brackets under its eaves, at Franklin and Pine Streets two blocks east of Central Square; now in commercial use.

places.name: Shoe Shop–Doucette Ten Footer
places.line: An 1850 backyard shoemaker's workshop, about 10 feet square, behind the Stoneham Historical Society at 36 William Street.

history.text: First settlement of the area known as Charlestown End.
The General Court granted separation from Charlestown on December 17, 1725.
A stagecoach line began serving the Medford to Andover Turnpike, and nearby farmland was divided into house lots.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Stoneham, MA?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, the median single-family sale price in Stoneham for calendar year 2025 was $805,000, across 130 sales. In 2024 it was $784,000, across 140 sales.
No station is located in Stoneham itself. Commuter rail stations in neighboring Melrose, Winchester, Wakefield and Woburn serve Boston's North Station, and Oak Grove on the Orange Line is in Malden.
Stoneham Public Schools. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: Did Stoneham ever have a train station?
faq.a: Yes. The Stoneham Branch of the Boston and Lowell Railroad was built to serve the town's shoe factories and carry passengers, and its 1895 brick depot still stands at Franklin and Pine Streets in commercial use. The Tri-Community Greenway now follows the branch's route, with its northern end at Gould Street across from Recreation Park.

notes: Condo figures set to null: the PDF's extracted text ends partway through the condo table (at Brookline), so Stoneham's condo rows could not be read. Settlement year conflicts (the town site says 1645, Wikipedia body says 1634), so the history uses the town site. The undated Housing Production Plan appears to date from about 2018, and its statement that most housing was built after 1960 was left out because it reads oddly against the town's history. The rail stations listed are representative stations in neighboring towns; Wikipedia names neighboring towns with stations but not specific nearest stations. Farm Hill is sourced to an independent local history site (bostonbasinhills.org), not an official one. Route 28 is listed from Wikipedia's note of a Route 28 exit and the Fells Reservoirs district boundary. Deepened 2026-10-22: added an overview paragraph on the Fells water-supply landscape (sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex_Fells_Reservoirs_Historic_District and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spot_Pond); places Boston and Maine Railroad Depot and Shoe Shop–Doucette Ten Footer; Haywardville as a (former) village; an FAQ on Stoneham's rail history (sources: the depot article and https://www.traillink.com/trail/tri-community-greenway/). To check: the Spot Pond article credits the reservoir works and 16-foot rise to the Metropolitan Water Supply Commission (1926 to 1946) while the district article credits the MDC, so the overview gives no date and names the MDC only for the pumping station; the Branch's opening and closing dates were not found in a page that loaded. The 1895 depot article does not name the line, so tying it to the Stoneham Branch is an inference. MBTA Communities was left out: a local news report describes a 7.6-acre district adopted in October 2022, but a town slide deck cites a 50-acre minimum, so the status is unclear.
